input.question: Low earth orbit speed is 15,430 mph to 17,450 mph. Escape speed must be higher. Why did it take Apollo missions three days to reach the moon, then, when it is only ~238,900 miles away?
input.ground_truth: Remember [Kepler's 2nd Law](_URL_1_) - orbits sweep out equal areas in equal time. For an elliptical orbit, such as a transfer orbit to the Moon, the effect of this law is that as you get further from Earth, the distance traveled along your orbit in a given time is less. So as the Apollo missions were traveling out to the Moon, they were constantly slowing down the entire time. By the time they were close enough to the Moon for the Moon's gravity to start pulling them inwards, [they were only traveling about 1113m/s](_URL_0_), or 2,489 mph.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Low earth orbit speed is 15,430 mph to 17,450 mph. Escape speed must be higher. Why did it take Apollo missions three days to reach the moon, then, when it is only ~238,900 miles away?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you want to throw a ball really, really far—like all the way to the next town, which is far away.

If you just throw the ball super hard, it will go fast, but then it will fall down to the ground because of gravity (the Earth pulls things back down). That’s like going fast but not fast enough to *leave* the Earth forever.

To get to the Moon, you don’t just need to go really fast—you need to go at the *right* speed and direction so you don’t fall back down and also don’t fly away forever. This special speed is called "escape velocity," and it’s even faster than just going around the Earth.

But the Apollo spaceship didn’t go straight to the Moon like a bullet. Instead, it went into a big circle around the Earth first (that’s called an "orbit"). Then, it slowly changed direction and speed, kind of like how you might steer a toy car in a circle and then point it toward another toy.

The Moon is far away (like 239,000 miles!), and even though the spaceship was going really fast (over 15,000 miles per hour!), it took three days to get there because:

1. It didn’t go in a straight line. It had to move into the right path.
2. It didn’t just zoom as fast as it could, because it had to save fuel and make sure it didn’t miss the Moon.
3. It was also moving around the Earth while trying to get to the Moon.

So, even though the Moon isn’t that much farther away than the speed the spaceship can go, it takes time to get there because of how space travel works!
